The structure is hiding behind ordinary words like need and willing. Once you see the flow underneath, a fast, correct algorithm comes for free.
Three stories that sound almost identical on the surface, and only one of them is genuinely hard.
Watch for the detail that actually changes the structure: how many groups, and how many choices does each rule touch at once?
answer: Pairing across two groups is bipartite, so a flow algorithm handles it. Pairing within one group is still solvable, just by a different, harder-to-implement method.
The third one is the trap: three variables per rule instead of two is the jump from an easy problem to a famously hard one.

lines: This is the first reduction run in the useful direction: toward an easy problem, to get a fast algorithm, rather than toward a hard one to prove difficulty.
Two independent checks landing on the identical number is the whole point. If a flow computation and a from-scratch search ever disagreed, one of them would have a bug.
The giveaway for this shape isn't the story, it's a yes-or-no test you can actually run on the graph: does every edge cross between two sides, with none staying inside one?
The moment that test fails, as it does for the odd cycle here, you're no longer looking at the easy version of this problem.
Watch how little this needs: no search over truth assignments at all, just following chains of implication through a graph and checking which ones loop back on themselves.
That's the whole trick behind why two choices per rule stays easy while three choices per rule becomes one of the hardest problems known.
The greedy rule here is almost suspiciously simple, finish earliest first, and yet it's provably as good as checking every possible combination.
That only holds because there's exactly one resource in play. The instant a second resource or a setup cost enters the story, this guarantee is gone.
Processing stages in an order where nothing ever points backward is what makes this relaxation correct and fast.
Add a single edge that loops back to an earlier stage, and you haven't just made this slower, you've left the territory where any fast, exact method is known to exist.
None of these six items are new ideas. Every one of them was built, proven and measured earlier in the course.
What's new is treating them as a lookup table: hear a question, and go straight to the technique that answers it, instead of reinventing it each time.
A small addition to the story, one cost for switching between jobs, and the clean guarantee from before quietly stops applying.
This is exactly the kind of detail a five-minute read has to catch, because the rest of the sentence can look completely unchanged.
answer: No, and the reason is structural, not just a matter of degree: the earlier guarantee relied on jobs being independent once ordered, with nothing coupling one job's finish to the next job's start.
Setup time breaks exactly that independence, which pushes the problem into the same hard family as bin packing and makespan scheduling.

lines: Notice this procedure ends on a falsifier, not on an answer. The last step is writing the one sentence that would prove the whole recognition wrong.
That habit is what keeps recognition honest. Anyone can spot a surface resemblance; writing down what would break it is what separates a real match from a near miss.
The point of scoring misses by what triggered them, rather than by whether the final answer was right, is that the same wrong trigger tends to repeat across many problems.
Fix the trigger once, and a whole category of future misses disappears with it.
Four topics, one underlying move: read the statement for what it actually permits, before reaching for any algorithm at all.

Everything from here was still a textbook object in a textbook problem. The next stretch of the course asks what each of these structures becomes once real stakes are attached to it. Hash tables inside hash joins, next.
